newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa rand seen stable below 4.50 in short-term.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa rand seen stable below 4.50 in short-term.

text.p: The rand is set to remain stable below 4.50 to the dollar in the short-term, despite its move into a slightly higher trading range this week, analysts said on Friday.
On Thursday, the rand touched its weakest level in five weeks when it sank to 4.4735 against the U.S. currency after trading in a 4.39 to 4.43 range since mid-March.
Currency traders have pinned the rand's slide largely on the dollar's rise to a 56-month high against the yen and a two-year high against the Deutschmark.
Boyde Stafne, technical analyst at UAL Merchant Bank Treasury, said technically the rand was now in a 4.43 to 4.47 trading range.
"From a technical point of view it has moved into a new trading range," Stafne said. "But it is not a big change from the previous one."
In the short-term, Stafne said that levels on the upside to watch were the 4.4838 or 4.5063 levels.

"There is a two-cent zone where I am expecting the dollar to top out. But the (recent) advance has not been a strong one so it might not even get there," he said, adding that only a move above those levels would force a rethink on his current bullish views on the currency.

Chris Tinker, at Standard Chartered in London, said for now the rand was in a broad 4.40 to 4.50 range, particularly as foreign investors would look to continue holding long rand positions to pick up the high yield.
"We know (Reserve Bank Governor Chris) Stals is concerned about the credit environment so interest rates are not going to come down quickly," Tinker said.
"There are encouraging direct investment flows but at the same time South Africa is running a trade balance which means it has to maintain those investment flows for a lot longer."

In that context, Tinker said the central bank would try to manage momentum and steady the currency, while using any rally to replenish its paltry gold and foreign exchange reserves, currently at just over 13 billion rand.
In the longer-term, Tinker said he expected the rand to move into a higher 4.50 to 4.75 range.
"The yield is high enough to prevent a wholesale sell-off and interest rates are high enough to prevent you having significant domestic credit extension problems and inflation."
A recent Reuters poll of economists forecast the rand would end the year at 4.73 against the dollar, largely in line with inflation differentials.
